title: Probability distributions and repeated observations
objectives: Validate a probability vector and calculate event probabilities.
Separate a model probability from a finite empirical frequency.
Calculate conditional probabilities from events and joint tables, including zero-probability boundaries.

quizzes.question: The envelope contains a recorded result, with pass labelled 0 and fail labelled 1. What does p=(3/4,1/4)ᵀ describe before opening it?
options: Our probabilities for the two recorded labels.
A coherent quantum superposition of pass and fail.
A guarantee that opening four envelopes produces exactly one failure.
feedback: Correct. It describes uncertainty about the classical label. Observing pass updates our information to (1,0)ᵀ without requiring the printed result to change.
The ket/column notation alone does not make a classical letter a quantum system. The entries here are probabilities, not amplitudes.
Expected proportions are not a guarantee about a finite batch. A batch also requires a specified repeated-preparation model.

quizzes.question: A model has P(1)=0.25, but a 100-trial batch contains 28 ones. What follows?
options: The observed frequency is 0.28; it can differ from the model probability.
The model has been proved false.
feedback: A finite frequency is an estimate, not a proof of the exact probability.
Correct. Interpreting the size of the discrepancy also requires the sampling assumptions and an uncertainty analysis.
This observation alone does not prove the model false. Finite samples fluctuate.
